questions.q: What is the difference between field-level and record-level completeness?
options: Field-level checks if a column has a value for a row; record-level checks if an entire expected record exists at all
Field-level only applies to numeric columns; record-level only applies to text columns
They are two names for exactly the same check
Field-level is measured with T-SQL; record-level can only be measured manually
questions.explain: Field-level completeness is about a single column having a value; record-level is about whether an entire expected row or record exists anywhere at all, often requiring a cross-table or cross-system comparison.

questions.q: Why does checking only `WHERE Email IS NULL` risk undercounting missing data?
options: It misses empty strings and sentinel values like 'N/A' that also represent missing data
IS NULL is not valid T-SQL syntax
It only works on the first row of a table
NULL values are always converted to zero automatically in SQL Server
questions.explain: An empty string is not NULL, so IS NULL misses it. Sentinel values like 'N/A' or '1900-01-01' look like real data to a plain count but represent the same missingness.

questions.q: In the per-column missingness query, what does the condition `LTRIM(RTRIM(PhoneNumber)) = ''` catch that `PhoneNumber IS NULL` alone would not?
options: Empty or whitespace-only strings stored in the column
Duplicate phone numbers
Phone numbers stored in the wrong format
Rows where PhoneNumber exceeds the column's maximum length
questions.explain: Trimming whitespace and comparing to an empty string catches blank-string values, which are a distinct form of missingness from a true NULL.

questions.q: What is the advantage of expressing completeness as a percentage rate rather than a one-time count?
options: A rate can be tracked over time and compared against a threshold on repeated runs
A rate is always more accurate than a count
SQL Server cannot return counts larger than 100
Rates eliminate the need for a reference table
questions.explain: A completeness rate, recalculated on a schedule, becomes a trackable metric you can monitor and threshold over time — unlike a single static count.

questions.q: Which example from the lesson illustrates a record-level completeness problem?
options: A customer placed an order, but no corresponding row exists in the Shipments table
A customer's Email column contains NULL
A customer's CountryCode column contains the sentinel value 'UNKNOWN'
A customer's PhoneNumber column contains an empty string
questions.explain: A missing row entirely — no Shipments record for an order that exists — is a record-level completeness problem, distinct from a missing value within an existing row (field-level).
